questions.stem: When is work done by a force on an object?

options.text: only when the object moves along the direction of the force
options.explanation: Movement through a distance along the force's line is the defining condition.

options.text: whenever a force is applied, moving or not
options.explanation: A force with no movement transfers nothing.

options.text: only when the force is very large
options.explanation: Size does not decide whether work happens; movement does.

options.text: only when the object speeds up afterwards
options.explanation: A change of speed is not required; any movement along the force counts.

questions.stem: A person applies a strong force to a heavy wall and nothing moves. How much work does the push do on the wall?

options.text: a small non-zero amount
options.explanation: With zero movement the work done on the wall is exactly zero.

options.text: none, because the wall never moves
options.explanation: No distance is covered, so no energy is transferred by the push.

options.text: a large amount, because the push is strong
options.explanation: Force size alone transfers nothing without movement.

options.text: an amount equal to the pusher's tiredness
options.explanation: Muscle effort is not the measure of mechanical work here.

questions.stem: A rope pulls a sledge forward, along its direction of travel. What happens to the sledge's stores?

options.text: its thermal store fills immediately and only
options.explanation: Heating of surroundings belongs to opposing forces, not the forward pull.

options.text: its stores stay exactly as they were
options.explanation: Work done along the motion always transfers energy in.

options.text: its kinetic store fills as energy is transferred to it
options.explanation: A force acting along the motion fills the mover's kinetic store.

options.text: its gravitational store empties as it is pulled
options.explanation: Nothing about the pull changes height.

questions.stem: A frictional force drags backwards on a moving cart, opposite to its motion. What does that force do?

options.text: it does no work because it opposes the motion
options.explanation: Opposing forces do work too — negative-direction work on the stores.

options.text: it adds energy to the cart's kinetic store
options.explanation: That is what an aligned force does, not an opposing one.

options.text: it only changes the cart's direction of travel
options.explanation: The cart keeps its heading; energy is what changes hands.

options.text: it removes energy from the cart, transferring it to the surroundings
options.explanation: An opposing force drains the mover's store and dissipates energy by heating.

questions.stem: Which unit counts both the work done by a force and the energy it transfers?

options.text: the joule
options.explanation: Work done and energy transferred share the joule.

options.text: the newton
options.explanation: Newtons measure force, not the transfer.

options.text: the watt
options.explanation: Watts measure power — energy transferred per second.

options.text: the kilogram
options.explanation: Kilograms measure mass.

questions.stem: State the condition under which a force does work on an object.
questions.modelAnswer: The object must move through a distance along the direction of the applied force; without that movement, no work is done.

questions.stem: State the relationship between the energy transferred when work is done and the size of that work.
questions.modelAnswer: The energy transferred is equal to the work done, and both quantities are measured in joules.

questions.stem: Explain why leaning against a closed door and pushing hard does no work on the door, even though your muscles tire.
questions.modelAnswer: Work requires the point of application of the force to travel some distance. The door stays closed and nothing moves, so no distance is covered, no energy is transferred by the push, and the work done on the door is zero — the tiredness comes from muscle chemistry, not from mechanical work.

questions.stem: A sledge is hauled 4 m forward along flat ground, then dragged 4 m back along the same path by an identical backward-acting frictional pull. Describe the work each force does.
questions.modelAnswer: The forward haul does work on the sledge and fills its kinetic store along the first leg, while the frictional drag acts opposite to the return motion, removing energy from the sledge and dissipating it to the thermal stores of the surroundings by heating.

questions.stem: A person slides a box forward along the floor. Where does the energy transferred by the pushing force end up?

options.text: entirely in the box's gravitational store
options.explanation: Height does not change on a level floor.

options.text: in the box's motion and in warming the box and floor
options.explanation: The aligned push fills the kinetic store; friction's opposing work warms the surfaces.

options.text: back inside the person's muscles, untouched
options.explanation: Energy leaves the person; it does not return by itself.

options.text: nowhere, because sliding costs nothing
options.explanation: Movement against any resistance always involves transfers.

questions.stem: A ball is lifted steadily upward. Which transfer does the lifting force perform?

options.text: an electrical transfer along the lifter's arm
options.explanation: The transfer route here is mechanical, not electrical.

options.text: no transfer, because the speed stays constant
options.explanation: Constant speed does not mean no transfer; height is changing.

options.text: a mechanical transfer into the ball's gravitational potential store
options.explanation: Lifting against gravity fills the gravitational store as height grows.

options.text: a heating transfer into the ball's thermal store
options.explanation: Steady lifting is not primarily a heating process.

questions.stem: A bird flies level at constant speed through still air. Which statement about its work is right?

options.text: it does no work because its speed is constant
options.explanation: Level flight still requires working against drag every second.

options.text: all its transferred energy goes to its gravitational store
options.explanation: Level flight changes no height.

options.text: the energy it spends returns to its kinetic store untouched
options.explanation: Drag constantly drains the store; the bird must keep refilling it.

options.text: it does work against air resistance, and that energy is dissipated to thermal stores
options.explanation: The bird pushes forward against drag, so energy drains from its kinetic store into warmth.

questions.stem: In the lifted-ball example, which statement about the stores is correct?

options.text: energy leaves the lifter and fills the ball's gravitational store
options.explanation: The lifting force does work and the height store fills.

options.text: energy multiplies as it passes between stores
options.explanation: Conservation forbids multiplication; amounts are transferred.

options.text: the ball's kinetic store grows while height increases at steady speed
options.explanation: Steady speed keeps the kinetic store level.

options.text: the surroundings gain nothing at all
options.explanation: Small heating effects are always present in real lifting.

questions.stem: Which everyday case involves a force doing work that immediately dissipates energy to the surroundings?

options.text: a satellite coasting far from any atmosphere
options.explanation: With no resistive force to work against, nothing dissipates.

options.text: a bird pushing through air resistance
options.explanation: Drag work ends as heating of the bird and the air.

options.text: a box resting untouched on the ground
options.explanation: No movement, no work.

options.text: a ball held motionless in an open hand
options.explanation: Holding still transfers no mechanical energy.

questions.stem: Name the store that fills when a ball is lifted to a height.
questions.modelAnswer: The ball's gravitational potential store fills as it is lifted higher in the gravitational field.

questions.stem: State which force a flying bird works against in level flight.
questions.modelAnswer: The bird does work against air resistance, also called drag, as it moves forward.

questions.stem: Explain why pushing a box along a rough floor warms the box and the floor slightly.
questions.modelAnswer: The pushing force does work as the box moves, and the rough surface drags against the motion. That opposing force also does work, taking energy from the box and dissipating it by heating to the thermal stores of the box and the floor.

questions.stem: A crane lifts a steel beam upward at constant speed. Compare the work done by the cable's pull with the work done by gravity on the beam.
questions.modelAnswer: The cable's upward pull does work along the lift and fills the beam's gravitational potential store, while gravity acts downward opposite the movement, doing work that drains that store — at constant speed the two effects balance, so the beam's kinetic store stays level.

questions.stem: Which product gives the work done by a steady force?

options.text: force × speed
options.explanation: Speed belongs to kinetic energy, not work done.

options.text: mass × distance moved
options.explanation: Mass never appears in the work done equation.

options.text: force × distance moved along the force
options.explanation: That product is exactly the energy the force transfers.

options.text: force ÷ distance moved
options.explanation: Dividing gives one rearrangement for finding force, not the definition.

questions.stem: A force of 20 N moves an object 3 m along the force's line. How much work is done?

options.explanation: That is 20 ÷ 3 — the wrong operation.
Adding the numbers is meaningless here.
No step of the calculation produces this value.
20 × 3 = 60, so 60 J of energy is transferred.

questions.stem: Which pair of units feeds W = F × d so the answer comes out in joules?

options.text: force in newtons, distance in metres
options.explanation: Newtons times metres gives joules (equivalently newton-metres).

options.text: force in newtons, time in seconds
options.explanation: Time is not part of work done.

options.text: mass in kilograms, distance in metres
options.explanation: Mass does not enter this equation.

options.text: force in newtons, distance in centimetres
options.explanation: Centimetres must be converted to metres first.

questions.stem: On the work done formula triangle, which arrangement is correct?

options.text: the triangle only works for speed, distance and time
options.explanation: The same triangle pattern serves many equations, including this one.

options.text: W on top, with F and d along the base
options.explanation: Covering W leaves F × d; covering F leaves W over d.

options.text: F on top, with W and d along the base
options.explanation: That layout would encode F = W × d, which is wrong.

options.text: d on top, with W and F along the base
options.explanation: That layout would encode d = W × F, which is wrong.

questions.stem: A crate is dragged 5 m along the floor, but the rope's tension acts at a slack angle so the crate's motion is only partly along the pull. What best describes the work done by the tension?

options.text: no work is done because of the angle
options.explanation: A partly-aligned force still does some work.

options.text: the work done doubles because of the angle
options.explanation: Angling reduces, never inflates, the along-force distance.

options.text: only the distance component along the pull counts toward the work done
options.explanation: The equation uses distance travelled in the force's own direction.

options.text: the full 5 m counts regardless of the angle
options.explanation: Off-axis movement earns nothing from that force.

questions.stem: State the work done equation using symbols, and name each quantity.
questions.modelAnswer: W = F × d, where W is the work done, F is the applied force and d is the distance the object travels along the force's line of action.

questions.stem: State the unit of work done and one equivalent combined unit.
questions.modelAnswer: Work done is measured in joules, which is equivalent to the newton-metre.

questions.stem: Explain why the distance must lie along the direction of the force for W = F × d to give the work done by that force.
questions.modelAnswer: The equation counts only the energy transfer caused by that particular force. Movement perpendicular to the force involves no push or drag along its line, so only distance travelled in the force's own direction represents energy moved by it.

questions.stem: The brakes of a van apply a force of 400 N and bring it to a stop over 30 m. Calculate the work done by the brakes.
questions.modelAnswer: W = F × d = 400 × 30 = 12 000 J, so the brakes transfer 12 000 J of energy while stopping the van.
